PRODUCTION NETWORKSResearch demonstration · 30 October 2026

TWO PERIODS AND AN INFINITE HORIZON

How do production links
change risk premia?

Compare sourcing arrangements and follow their effects on risk compensation. The two-period model explains the basic channels; the infinite-horizon model adds ongoing investment and persistent productivity shocks.

INFINITE HORIZON · TWO SECTORS · SAME STEADY SECTOR SIZES

What does persistence change in the two-sector example?

Keep the two sectors and their production parameters. Allow production and investment to continue each quarter. Balanced sourcing preserves sector sizes: the network changes the distribution of risk compensation while the aggregate capital premium remains unchanged in this local model.

Stylized theory · No empirical calibration · Leading covariance premia, annualized in basis points

OPTIONAL EXTENSIONThree sectors: does network position change the premium?Compare hubs, directed cycles and dispersed links at fixed sector sizes and shock moments.

Follow the same sector across different sourcing arrangements. Its consumption share, steady capital stock, Domar weight and productivity process stay fixed. Among the linked arrangements, total spending on other sectors’ inputs also stays fixed.

This is a separate three-sector economy, with shares (60%, 30%, 10%) and Domar weights (1.2, 0.6, 0.2). Comparing its premium levels with the two-sector economy would also change the size and diversification of shocks. The controlled comparison here is across three-sector networks.

Preferences and shock moments — applied identically to every network

One correlation applies to all three pairs; −0.5 is its lowest admissible value. The common factor is independent and loads equally on all sectors. All four factors share persistence ρ. These controls change shocks jointly for every network; they never move a shock to a different sector when its network position changes.

The same technology and quarterly preferences as the two-sector infinite model: α = 0.33, η = 0.50, ξ = 0.17, β = 0.99, δ = 0.025 and χ = 3.5. These controls are independent of the two-sector controls below.

Which shock exposures account for the difference?

Return responses and their contributions to the selected sector’s premium
ShockReturn response A (%)Return response B (%)Premium A (bp)Premium B (bp)Difference (bp)

Each return response is to a positive 1% innovation, with inherited capital fixed and equilibrium investment adjusting. The premium contribution uses the selected covariance, so it is zero for a zero-variance shock even if its return response is nonzero. With correlated innovations, contributions include cross-covariances and are an accounting decomposition, not independent causal channels.

Annual RPj = −40,000 bRj Σ bMContribution of return exposure to shock i = −40,000 bRji(Σ bM)i

bRji is sector j’s log-return response to innovation i; bM is the vector of log-SDF responses; Σ is the innovation covariance matrix. Consumption and continuation-value responses, and hence bM, are identical across these networks. The premium differences therefore come from return exposure.

All arrangements at the same shock settings

Premium changes relative to own-sector sourcing, annual bp
ArrangementSector 1Sector 2Sector 3Aggregate

All six linked arrangements spend 16% of total intermediate expenditure across sectors. Hub arrangements split this spending equally across four directed links; cycles split it equally across three; dispersed sourcing splits it equally across all six. Across these arrangements, partner identity, concentration and each sector’s cross-sector share can change. Reversing the directed cycle keeps each sector’s own-input share and number of purchasing and selling links fixed; only the direction and identity of its trading partners change. It does not isolate a single centrality statistic. A pure one-way chain cannot satisfy the required balance at these fixed sizes.

Why this holds sector sizes fixed, and what the result establishes
θ = (0.6, 0.3, 0.1),   W1 = 1,   θ′W = θ′Fij = θiWij,   Σi≠j Fij = 0.16 for every linked arrangementℓ = θ/(1 − η) = (1.2, 0.6, 0.2)0.6 ΔRP1 + 0.3 ΔRP2 + 0.1 ΔRP3 = 0

W records input expenditure shares. F records shares of total intermediate spending. Balance means each sector’s intermediate purchases and sales have the same value at the steady state. Own-sector purchases fill the remaining budget. With common production parameters and reference productivity one, steady prices equal one, primitive CES weights equal W, and steady capital and Domar weights remain identical across arrangements. After shocks, expenditure shares adjust with prices unless σ = 1.

The aggregate invariance argument in the two-sector model extends to three sectors. Common technology and balanced sourcing make the aggregate linear system independent of W, so the network changes sector compensation while leaving its capital-weighted average unchanged. This conclusion is conditional on those assumptions and the local approximation.

At the default settings, moving the hub from sector 1 to sector 3 lowers sector 3’s premium by 2.288 annual bp. At σ = 2, the same change raises it by 1.508 bp. Reversing the buyer-to-supplier cycle from 1 → 2 → 3 → 1 to 1 → 3 → 2 → 1 raises sector 3’s premium by 9.422 bp at the default settings, while preserving each sector’s own-input share and number of trading partners. Network position affects exposure to priced shocks; being the hub does not imply a uniformly higher premium. Equal sector sizes combined with equal independent sector shocks would eliminate these local network premium effects under the maintained common technology, even for different balanced arrangements. Unequal fixed sizes make the illustrated shock exposures economically distinct.

These are comparisons of specified economies, not a theorem that a given centrality measure orders premia. Comparing two different sectors within one arrangement still mixes size and network position. The A–B comparison follows the same sector.

Accuracy and approximation

The page uses first-order equilibrium responses and leading second-order covariance premia. It does not solve risk-adjusted mean capital or a global nonlinear equilibrium. The external adjustment-cost convention and revenue-share feedback are retained. A quarterly covariance is multiplied by 40,000 to report an annual rate in basis points; this is not an exact annual holding-period excess return. No full shock distribution or empirical calibration is imposed.

Both sectors retain α = 0.33, η = 0.50 and labor share ξ = 0.17. Consumption weights are 80% and 20%; quarterly β = 0.99, depreciation δ = 0.025, and external adjustment-cost exponent χ = 3.5. The same ρ applies to both sector productivity factors and the common factor. Innovation correlation is a different parameter.

Structural controls select from 1,584 verified local equilibrium responses. Shock scales, correlation and risk aversion recalculate covariance premia from those responses without interpolation. Risk aversion and shock variance do not change first-order policies; higher-order precautionary changes in investment are not solved.

WHAT CARRIES OVER FROM THE TWO-PERIOD EXAMPLE?

Same sectors and primitives; a continuing capital claim

The main examples in both tabs use two sectors, common capital and intermediate shares, Cobb–Douglas consumption, CES intermediate inputs, Epstein–Zin preferences and the same external adjustment-cost convention. To compare network effects, use “Same reference Domar weights” in the two-period tab, with intensity 0.4 and the same remaining parameters.

FeatureTwo periodsInfinite horizon
ProductionLabor and investment initially; neither at the terminal dateLabor, production and investment every quarter
Capital payoffTerminal residual profitRental income plus undepreciated resale value
Capital referenceInherited initial stocks; saving determines terminal capitalEndogenous steady state and local dynamic adjustment
UncertaintyOne uncertain terminal dateRepeated innovations, possibly persistent
UnitsPercent per unspecified model periodAnnualized covariance premium from a quarterly model

These changes are required to continue the economy. Levels across tabs are not a pure decomposition of the horizon effect. The 5% shock scale is retained as an illustrative quarterly input, not obtained by converting the two-period model’s unspecified period into a quarter. Matching the same reference purchase shares across horizons need not imply identical primitive CES weights, because terminal reference prices can differ.

Equations and interpretation

Why is the aggregate network effect zero here?

This follows from common sector parameters and balanced sourcing, not fixed Domar weights alone. Let k̄, ȳ and z̄ denote θ-weighted sector log deviations; let K* and R* denote steady aggregate capital and gross revenue, and C* steady consumption.

(1 − η)ȳt = z̄t + αk̄t(1 − η)R*ȳt = C*ĉt + K*[(1 + χδ)k̄t+1 − (1 − δ + χδ)k̄t]

Since θ′W = θ′ and θ-weighted goods-price changes sum to zero, the network drops out of aggregate linear production, resource and capital-pricing equations. Aggregate consumption, continuation-value news and capital-return news are unchanged across balanced networks facing the same shocks.

0.8 ΔRP1 + 0.2 ΔRP2 = 0,   ΔRP2 = −4 ΔRP1

Persistence can change the aggregate premium itself, but equally under both sourcing arrangements. This is a local aggregation result under common parameters, not a general theorem about networks or nonlinear finite-risk premia.

Preferences, capital returns and adjustment costs
Mt+1 = β(Ct+1/Ct)−1/ψ(Vt+1/μt)1/ψ−γRkj,t+1 = [αpj,t+1yj,t+1/Kj,t+1 + (1 − δ)qj,t+1] / qjtgjt = Kj,t+1/Kjt,   qjt = pjtgjtχIjt = Kj,t+1 − (1 − δ)Kjt,   goods used = gjtχIjt

M is the SDF; C is consumption; V is recursive utility; μ is its conditional Epstein–Zin certainty equivalent. γ denotes risk aversion, ψ the EIS and β the discount factor. p and q are goods and capital prices in consumption units. Capital producers take sector-wide growth g as given privately under the retained Kekre–Lenel convention; aggregate resource use includes its cost.

The ongoing recursive SDF uses β. The two-period SDF uses β/(1 − β) because terminal continuation utility is consumption. Reusing the terminal factor in an ongoing economy would be incorrect.

Shock persistence, variance and annualization
log zjt = at + ujtat+1 = ρat + εa,t+1,   uj,t+1 = ρujt + εj,t+1Σinnovation = Σscale   (fixed innovations)Σinnovation = (1 − ρ²)Σscale   (fixed long-run variances)

Scale controls specify log standard deviations in percent. At ρ = 0 they are both innovation and stationary-factor standard deviations. The common innovation is independent of the sector innovations; sector correlation is separately selectable. No full probability distribution is imposed.

Annual RPj (bp) = −4 × 10,000 × Covt(log Mt+1, log Rkj,t+1)

This is a quarterly covariance premium at an annual rate, not an exact annual holding-period or arithmetic excess return. At a given ρ, fixed-long-run-variance premia equal (1 − ρ²) times their fixed-innovation counterparts because shock scale leaves first-order policies unchanged.

What survives, and what remains conditional?

With baseline parameters and independent equal sector shocks, the balanced network lowers sector 1’s premium and raises sector 2’s. With long-run variance fixed, sector 2’s effect rises from 1.052 basis points at ρ = 0 to 7.936 at ρ = 0.95, then falls to 7.688 at ρ = 0.98. Persistence does not imply monotonic amplification.

The sector sign is not universal: at input elasticity σ = 2 the baseline signs reverse. At σ = 1, sector effects remain despite constant intermediate expenditure shares. With only an equally loading common shock, network effects vanish under the maintained symmetric technology.

Policies are first-order and covariance premia are leading second-order terms. Risk-adjusted mean capital, higher-order state-dependent premia and a global nonlinear equilibrium are not solved. Large shocks and high persistence can make local magnitudes unreliable. Reducing all shock standard deviations tenfold divides leading premia and effects by 100, preserving signs.

Numerical verification

All 1,584 structural cases satisfy the steady-size restrictions and have stable transition roots. Maximum linear Euler residual: 3.0 × 10−13. Forty-eight cases were independently checked with the older nonlinear static solver and numerical derivatives; the largest premium discrepancy was 0.000013 annual basis points. Additional checks cover production, resources, labor, household budgets, zero risk, covariance scaling, common shocks and alternative parameters. Saved scenarios include units, inputs, source hashes and the verification summary.

THE TWO-PERIOD MODEL

Saving today, uncertain profits tomorrow

Saving and investment adjust · Second-order expectations · One period, without annualization

The total effect includes changes in sector size. Matching reference Domar weights asks whether sourcing matters beyond that size channel.

1. Production links

Move from own-sector inputs to your chosen sourcing arrangement.

Sourcing weights describe the technology. Actual expenditure shares also depend on equilibrium goods prices.

2. Uncertainty

Standard deviations of log productivity, in percent per period.

The common shock affects both sectors equally and is independent of the two sector-specific shocks. Correlation applies to the sector-specific shocks.

3. Demand and technology

Terminal technology requires α + η < 1.

4. Preferences, capital and productivity

Capital controls are inherited stocks at the start of date 0. The economy chooses the stocks carried into date 1.

5. Saving and investment

The slides assign utility weights 1 − β and β to the two dates. Their implied relative weight is β / (1 − β): at β = 0.99, this is 99, not 0.99. Date-0 labor supply is one; date-0 productivity is normalized to one.

READING THE NETWORK CONTROLS

What does τ change?

τ (tau) measures how far the sourcing arrangement moves toward your target: 0 means own-sector inputs; 1 means the target network. At 0.5, the cross-sector weights or shares being varied are halfway to their targets. Each value describes a separate economy; τ is not time or shock persistence.

How is the target chosen when Domar weights are matched?
θ1W12 = θ2W21
W*12 = s min(1, θ2/θ1)W*21 = s min(1, θ1/θ2)

θ1 = θ and θ2 = 1 − θ are consumption expenditure shares. The intensity s selects the target: s = 1 gives the largest cross-sector purchases consistent with the match. The program solves for technology weights that deliver these purchase shares at equilibrium prices. After a productivity shock, technology weights stay fixed and purchase shares can change.

CHOICES BEFORE THE SHOCKS

How do saving and investment respond?

Initial goods prices, consumption, investment and sector asset prices solve goods clearing, labor clearing and household Euler equations together. Expectations are approximated to second order using the chosen shock covariance.

Initial-period equilibrium
QuantityOwn-sectorYour network
Isolating the additional effect of capital reallocation
Linked economy’s premium (%)Sector 1Sector 2

What does “second order” mean here?

The household’s expected discounted payoffs are expanded through shock variances and covariances. We solve those approximated Euler equations jointly with the exact resource accounts. No Gaussian distribution is imposed. This is a local approximation, not an exact solution for arbitrarily large shocks.

The main charts evaluate the local covariance premium at the risk-adjusted capital solution. A strictly leading-order premium instead evaluates it at the zero-risk investment equilibrium. Their difference consists of higher-order terms, so it should not be interpreted as additional second-order precision.

Who buys from whom?

Actual intermediate expenditure shares

Buyer ↓ / supplier →Sector 1Sector 2

Arrows run from supplier to buyer. Own-sector purchases are included in the table.

Wjk = ωjkpk1−σ / (∑l ωjlpl1−σ)

Wjk is the fraction of buyer j’s intermediate spending paid to supplier k. It depends on the technology weight ωjk, suppliers’ prices p, and the substitution elasticity σ. Thus a technology weight of 0.5 need not imply a purchase share of 50%.

Consumption risk and sector exposure
QuantityOwn-sectorYour network
RPj ≡ −Cov(log M, log Rj)= γ Cov(log C1, log Rj)= bjC γ Var(log C1)

RPj is the covariance premium; M is the household’s stochastic discount factor, Rj is sector j’s gross return, C1 is terminal consumption, and γ is risk aversion. Cov measures comovement across possible shocks; Var measures risk. A return that falls when consumption is low requires a positive premium.

bjC = Cov(log Rj, log C1) / Var(log C1)

The consumption beta bjC measures return exposure to consumption risk. It is different from the preference parameter β and is undefined when consumption has zero variance. The page evaluates these covariances using local responses to productivity shocks and reports 100 × RPj, in percent per period. These are approximate covariance premia, not exact arithmetic excess returns.

What this demonstration establishes

Production links can change the amount of consumption risk and each sector’s exposure to it. With endogenous investment, they also change the capital allocation before the shocks occur. The sign and the sector ranking depend on technology, final demand and the distribution of productivity shocks. These are local, illustrative model calculations, not estimates of US premia.

Guide to the symbols and controls

There are two dates, 0 and 1, and two sectors, indexed by j and k. Network parameter τ compares different economies; it does not index dates.

Symbols used on this page
SymbolMeaning
τ (tau), sProgress toward the target network; target cross-sector intensity in the matched-Domar comparison.
Ω, ωjk; W, WjkTechnology weights; actual intermediate expenditure shares. Buyer j purchases from supplier k. A star marks the target matrix; I without a subscript is the identity matrix.
θ (theta)Sector 1’s share of consumption expenditure. Sector 2 has share 1 − θ. In matrix equations, θ denotes the vector of both shares.
α (alpha), η (eta)Capital and intermediate-input exponents in terminal production: yj = zjKjαMjη. Their sum must be below one.
σ (sigma)Elasticity of substitution between intermediate goods. Values below one mean inputs are harder to substitute; σ = 1 is Cobb–Douglas.
σ1, σ2, σaStandard deviations of the two sector-specific shocks and the common shock. These subscripted symbols describe uncertainty, not substitution. Inputs are in percent; the model converts them to log units.
ρ (rho)Correlation between the two sector-specific shocks. It is not persistence over time; this model has one uncertain terminal date.
γ (gamma)Risk aversion: the strength of the household’s aversion to uncertainty in terminal consumption.
β (beta), ψ (psi)Future utility weight and intertemporal elasticity of substitution. The latter describes willingness to shift consumption across dates. The relative utility weight on date 1 is β/(1 − β).
δ (delta), χ (chi)Depreciation and the external adjustment-cost exponent. Initial investment is Ij = Kj − (1 − δ)Kj,old; its price is qj = pj0(Kj/Kj,old)χ.
zj, Kj, MjSector productivity, terminal capital and the intermediate-input composite. Capital controls specify inherited stocks in the investment mode and terminal stocks in the fixed-capital mode.
ℓj, bjC, RPjDomar weight, consumption beta and covariance risk premium. Consumption beta is an exposure measure, distinct from preference parameter β.
M, μThe stochastic discount factor and the certainty equivalent of terminal consumption. M without a subscript prices uncertain payoffs; Mj denotes production inputs.

Shock covariance matrix Σ (capital sigma) combines common and sector-specific uncertainty:

Σ11 = σa² + σ1²,   Σ22 = σa² + σ2²Σ12 = Σ21 = σa² + ρσ1σ2

The common shock is independent of the sector-specific shocks. The page uses their variances and covariance, without assuming a full probability distribution.

What does keeping Domar weights fixed mean?

A terminal Domar weight is gross sector revenue divided by the value of final consumption: ℓ = (I − ηW′)−1θ. Because gross revenue includes intermediate transactions, Domar weights need not sum to one. With the common intermediate exponent here, each sector’s share of total gross revenue is (1 − η)ℓj.

The total-effect comparison holds preferences, demand, technology exponents and shock moments fixed while changing primitive sourcing weights. Equilibrium sector sizes can change. The matched comparison instead chooses sourcing technologies that preserve the own-sector reference Domar weights θ/(1 − η). Demand and shock parameters are not recalibrated to force the match.

For two sectors, the restriction is θ1W12 = θ2W21. One cross-sector intensity therefore determines both actual expenditure shares. At intensity s and progress τ, W12 = τs min(1, θ2/θ1) and W21 = τs min(1, θ1/θ2). The program finds the primitive CES weights consistent with these shares and equilibrium prices. With endogenous investment, it solves the matching condition jointly with the initial equilibrium.

Matching holds at the terminal reference equilibrium used in the main charts. It does not fix absolute revenues, market capitalizations, initial-period sector sizes or revenues in every shock realization. After a shock, technology weights stay fixed and actual expenditure shares respond to prices. These different responses are precisely what can generate different premia.

At matched Domar weights and unchanged shock moments, the local consumption-risk component and the reference revenue-weighted average premium are identical across the two economies. Any main-chart premium difference comes from relative return exposure. This is a test of differences across sectors, not a test of whether links raise average compensation for aggregate risk. Matching removes an economically meaningful part of the total network effect; neither comparison is universally better. The chosen balanced sourcing path is a different counterfactual from the unrestricted path; it is not a unique decomposition of that original experiment.

The match is imposed at risk-adjusted capital when investment is endogenous. The separate strictly leading-order check keeps the same primitive technology and evaluates zero-risk capital; its Domar weights can differ by higher-order terms. Changing initial conditions or investment preferences may change the required technology weights while leaving the main-chart terminal exposures fixed by the selected expenditure shares.

Equations and assumptions

There are two sectors. Terminal production is yj = zjkjαMjη, with α + η < 1. The intermediate composite is CES with elasticity σ. Household consumption is Cobb–Douglas with expenditure shares θ and 1 − θ. Capital is predetermined when the terminal shocks arrive; there is no terminal labor or investment, and the terminal residual payoff is (1 − η)pjyj.

In the total-effect mode, the primitive sourcing matrix is Ω(τ) = (1 − τ)I + τΩ*. The target off-diagonal weights are ω12 and ω21. Actual shares satisfy Wjk = ωjkpk1−σ / Σlωjlpl1−σ. Each comparison recomputes goods prices, expenditure shares and the terminal allocation.

Write L = I − ηW, A = L−1, ℓ = A′θ, ν = (1 − η)ℓ and S = diag(ν). The corrected response uses D = diag(W′ν) − W′SW, H = η(1 − σ)S−1A′D and B = L − (1 − η)H. Consumption responds with ℓ′, log returns with F = 1ℓ′ − HB−1, and log goods prices with G = −B−1 + 1ℓ′. Here ν denotes gross revenue shares, distinct from depreciation δ. Revenue-share feedback is retained.

The covariance premium is RP = γFΣℓ. In percentage units, the page reports 100 × RP. It is the local approximation to E[log R] − log Rf + ½Var(log R), rather than an exact finite-risk arithmetic excess return. There is no annualization. Large shock scales can make a local approximation less informative.

Productivity is log zj = log z̄j + a + εj, where z̄ is the reference productivity setting. The common component a is independent of ε; Corr(ε1, ε2) is adjustable. Thus Σ11 = σa² + σ1², Σ22 = σa² + σ2² and Σ12 = σa² + ρσ1σ2. All covariances refer to the same period.

Demand shares remain strictly positive so both sectors are active in the own-sector benchmark. The common capital exponent, intermediate exponent and substitution elasticity follow the existing analytical model. Their sector-specific generalization would require a new derivation.

Initial-period equations and the approximation

Date-0 production uses inherited capital, labor and intermediates, with labor exponent ξ = 1 − α − η and aggregate labor fixed at one. The date-0 productivity level is one. Investment is Ij = Kj − (1 − δ)Kj,old. Under the retained Kekre–Lenel external-cost convention, qj = pj0(Kj/Kj,old)χ and investment absorbs (Kj/Kj,old)χIj units of good j. Capital producers take sector-wide growth as given. Disinvestment is permitted, as in the maintained convention.

The terminal claim pays πj = (1 − η)pj1yj1/Kj, preserving the slides’ residual-profit payoff. The SDF is M = [β/(1 − β)]C01/ψμγ−1/ψC1−γ, where μ is the Epstein–Zin certainty equivalent. The system imposes qj ≈ E[Mπj] using a second-order expansion of log expectations. This is a decentralized equilibrium calculation, not a planner problem that internalizes the investment externality.

Let c = log C1 and dj = log πj. At the reference terminal equilibrium, their gradients are ℓ and fj, and their Hessians are Qc and Qj. The certainty-equivalent correction is u = ½ tr(QcΣ) + ½(1 − γ)ℓ′Σℓ. The log-pricing correction is aj = (γ − 1/ψ)u + ½ tr[(Qj − γQc)Σ] + ½(fj − γℓ)′Σ(fj − γℓ). The solver uses log qj = log[β/(1 − β)] + (log C0 − c̄)/ψ + d̄j + aj.

Patience and the EIS now affect saving and investment. They can change network premia through the resulting capital allocation and terminal expenditure shares. The fixed-capital mode intentionally has no such channel. Shock persistence remains absent because there is only one uncertain terminal date; the controls specify its conditional covariance directly.

The deterministic and stochastic reference equilibria are numerical solutions, not a general uniqueness theorem. Small residuals establish the equations of the local approximation, not its accuracy for arbitrarily large shocks or unspecified higher moments.
